newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic kicks off election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic kicks off election campaign.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic on Thursday kicked off his ruling Socialist Party's election campaign by accusing foreign powers and the Serbian opposition of working together to destabilise the country.
All such efforts by "certain outside factors with the help of some internal ones" had failed, Milosevic said in a rare public appearance in the central Serbian town of Arandjelovac.
"No one outside the country can decide on changes in it, only its own citizens can," he added.

Milosevic was referring to the massive protests in Belgrade and across Serbia organised by the opposition coalition Zajedno after authorities cancelled its victories in local elections in the 14 biggest Serbian towns and cities last November.
After three months, Milosevic caved in to continuous street demonstrations and intense international pressure by recognising the opposition poll victories. The Socialists' popularity plunged.
Serbian presidential and parliamentary elections are due to be held by the end of the year.

In a bid to bolster its flagging popularity ahead of the elections, Milosevic shuffled the Socialist leadership in April and restored Milorad Vucelic as party vice-president, to be practically in charge of the campaign.
Vucelic was dismissed from the party leadership after the Dayton peace talks on Bosnia late in 1995 because of his nationalist stance.
Diplomats and opposition leaders believe his re-emergence shows that Milosevic will once again bank on nationalism as his campaign ticket.
Milosevic has postponed until after the elections privatisations of the near-bankrupt economy, which he had promised this year, authoritative sources said.

Milosevic cannot run for a third term as Serbian president. Analysts and diplomats believe he will instead go for the post of federal president of Yugoslavia, which now comprises only Serbia and Montenegro, but with greater powers than the chiefly ceremonial ones held by the incumbent Zoran Lilic.
Diplomats said Milosevic had little to fear electorally from Zajedno, which looked so threatening last winter.
Continuous disputes among the Zajedno leaders have eroded much of their popularity.
"I did not freeze my butt for three months and get beaten up by the cops (on demonstrations) just so those people could feel important," Zoran Stankovic, a Belgrade student, said.

He was referring to Zoran Djindjic, leader of the Democratic Party and now Belgrade mayor, Vesna Pesic, a Nobel peace prize nominee, and Vuk Draskovic, the leader of the Serbian Renewal Movement and Zajedno's presidential candidate.
Most diplomats believe the coalition will fall apart due to rivalry between Djindjic and Draskovic.
